title: How can some centenarians lead unhealthy lives?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how some centenarians live long lives despite unhealthy habits, using Madame Jeanne Calment (smoked until 100, died at 122) as a starting point. They cover genetics and family clustering of centenarians, caloric restriction in rats and worms, longevity genes (SIRT1, FOXO3A, IGF-1 with Ashkenazi Jewish women), Dawkins' gene-vessel idea and Ruth Hardy's theory on women's longevity genes, the Hayflick limit on cell division, and the historical case of Old Tom Parr, who lived to about 152 and was taken to court by King Charles I. The episode also includes a plug for the Super Stuff Guide to the Economy audiobook, a blog mention, and a listener letter from a postal worker about junk mail funding the Postal Service.
topics: junk mail and the Postal Service

segments.title: Opening banter and Madame Clement
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode, joke about the cold and the death-themed episodes, and Josh introduces Madame Jeanne Clement, who smoked until 100 and died at 122. They discuss Josh's own unhealthy habits and the idea of living a long life, and Chuck's grandmother who lived to 100 or older.

segments.title: Genes and caloric restriction
segments.summary: They discuss family clustering of centenarians as evidence for genetic influence, and how caloric restriction in rats and other animals leads to longer, healthier lives, including the role of fat storage and survival mode.

segments.title: SIRT1, FOXO3A and other longevity genes
segments.summary: They describe the SIRT1 gene, which inhibits the BAX protein that triggers programmed cell death, and the FOXO3A gene, which affected worm lifespan and was found in elderly Japanese and German people. They also mention the IGF-1 gene mutation found in Ashkenazi Jewish women and the cancer-related explanation for it.

segments.title: Dawkins' gene theory, women and longevity, and the Hayflick limit
segments.summary: They discuss Richard Dawkins' view that organisms are vessels for their genes, and a theory by Ruth Hardy about why women might carry longevity genes that men do not. They then cover the Hayflick limit, the roughly fifty divisions a cell can make before stopping, and Hayflick's nucleus-replacement experiment.

segments.title: Old Tom Parr
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck tell the story of Old Tom Parr, born around 1483, who lived as a single man until 80, then married and had children, fathered an illegitimate child at about 100, and reportedly lived to 152. They describe how a disgraced courtier brought him to the court of King Charles, where he partied heavily and died.

segments.title: Audiobook and blog plugs
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh promote the Super Stuff Guide to the Economy audiobook on iTunes and mention the show blog and Friday recap.
topics: Super Stuff Guide to the Economy

segments.title: Listener mail on junk mail and the Postal Service
segments.summary: A letter carrier named Scott writes that junk mail is a major source of revenue for the US Postal Service and helps keep postal jobs, responding to the hosts' earlier junk mail episode. Josh notes recent Postal Service layoffs.
